question: Which design decisions in foundation models (training data, architecture, scale, post-training, sampling) matter for downstream application builders?
contributions: Explains how training data distribution shapes capability, with multilingual and domain-specific cases
Walks through the transformer, its alternatives, scale measures, scaling laws and bottlenecks
Describes SFT and preference finetuning (RLHF) as post-training
Treats sampling (temperature, top-k, top-p, test time compute, structured outputs) and the probabilistic nature of models, including inconsistency and hallucination

limits: Author states the chapter cannot say how to build a model competing with ChatGPT; training details are confidential or skipped
Time-bound: prices ($2 to $5 per H100 hour), logprob API availability, and 'as of this writing' claims have dated
Scaling law is for dense models on mostly human-generated data; sparse and synthetic data adaptation is an open question
RLHF and DPO covered shallowly; equations for attention and reward loss do not extract from the PDF text
Many numbers are relayed from other work (Lai 2023, Yennie Jun, Cobbe 2021); the chapter runs no experiments
practices: Choose training data to match your task, language and domain; a smaller high-quality set can beat a larger low-quality one (Training Data).
For non-English applications, check tokenization cost and quality per language rather than translating everything to English (Multilingual Models).
Budget from compute: pick model size and tokens with the Chinchilla ~20 tokens per parameter rule, then consider inference cost (Scaling law).
Track three scale numbers: parameters, training tokens, FLOPs (Model Size).
Use test time compute (best of N, verifier, majority vote) to improve quality, knowing cost scales with N (Test Time Compute).
Fix temperature, top-p, top-k, and seed for consistency, but expect residual non-determinism (Inconsistency).
For structured outputs escalate: prompting, post-processing, test time compute, constrained sampling, finetuning (Structured Outputs).
Set max tokens carefully so JSON is not truncated (Structured Outputs).
Look at logprobs when debugging a model (Temperature tip).

terms.definition: The model processes the input tokens in parallel, creating the key and value vectors for all input tokens.
The model generates one output token at a time.
FLOPs measure the compute requirement for a task, whereas FLOP/s measures a machine's peak performance.
How much of the maximum compute capacity you can use.
A model that achieves the best performance given a fixed compute budget.
(prompt, response) examples used for SFT; also called behavior cloning.
(prompt, winning_response, losing_response) used to train a reward model.
Always picking the most likely outcome.
Probabilities in the log scale, preferred to reduce underflow.
Sum probabilities in descending order and stop when the sum reaches p; consider only those values.
Generating multiple responses per query to increase the chance of a good one.
A response that isn't grounded in facts.
A model generates very different responses for the same or slightly different prompts.
